chapter_title: Rama to the Rescue (Fables and Folk Tales)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Into the Comic Strip: Reading and First Response

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.22): identify odd character and intruder from first comic sequence.
Let us discuss (p.23): true or false — man's plan and thief's wish.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the comic strip format and its Tamil Nadu folk-tale origin. Read the first two sequences aloud with the class, pointing out the husband, wife, and the thief entering through a dug hole.

Work through 'Let us discuss' on p.22: class identifies the odd character (children are not present) and who entered the house (the robber, not the kotwal). Discuss how the comic panels convey this without dialogue.

Continue reading the second sequence. Students write True or False for the two statements on p.23 — whether the man shares his plan with his wife, and what the thief hopes to overhear. Discuss answers as a class, drawing attention to the whispered plan panel.

periods.teacher_notes: The comic-strip format means meaning is split between speech bubbles and visual panels; prompt students to read both together rather than only the text. The thief's frustration at hearing domestic chatter instead of money talk is a key story beat — ensure students notice the contrast between what he hopes to hear and what the couple actually says.
materials: Textbook pp.20–23 (comic strip, 'Let us discuss' exercises)

periods.activity_title: Predicting, Matching, and Mapping the Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.24): call 'Rama' at three volumes; predict what happens next.
Let us discuss (p.25): match six words in Column A with meanings in Column B.
Let us discuss (p.26): fill story-map boxes — characters, setting, problem, solution.

time_bands.activity: Read the mid-story sequence aloud to the class. Then invite the whole class to call out the name 'Rama' together — softly, then loudly, then very loudly — as directed on p.24, and ask students to predict what will happen next in the story.

Read the final sequences to complete the story. Students then work on the matching task on p.25, pairing six words (wonder, yard, chatter, instead, closely, perhaps) with their meanings. Correct orally as a class.
Students fill the story-map on p.26 with suitable words for Main Characters, Setting, Other Characters, Problem, and Solution. Pairs share their maps and the class agrees on a consensus version.

periods.teacher_notes: The volume-variation call of 'Rama' is the story's central clever device — the wife's graduated loudness acts as a location signal to the kotwal without alarming the thief. Ensure students connect this moment to the plan the husband whispered earlier so the story's logic is clear before they attempt the story-map.
materials: Textbook pp.24–26 (comic strip conclusion, matching task, story-map)

periods.activity_title: Close Reading: Extract Analysis and Reflective Questions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.26–27): extract questions on two passages — meaning, character inference.
Let us think and reflect II (p.27): short and extended answer questions on plot and theme.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect II (p.27): write a paragraph on whether cleverness can solve problems, with a reason.

time_bands.activity: Read the first extract (pp.26–27) aloud: the opening exchange between husband and wife about the noise. Students answer the three sub-questions — why the man speaks first, the meaning of 'Ssssh', and how the panel shows the wife listening carefully. Discuss as a class.

Read the second extract (p.27) about the kotwal running to the house. Students answer the three sub-questions — filling the blank, the meaning of 'Oh, Oh!', and how the kotwal's behaviour shows professional competence. Compare the two extracts' use of exclamation.

Students individually answer the three short-answer questions on p.27 (why they couldn't sleep, what the thief wished for, how they got help) and share answers aloud. The final reflective question — whether cleverness solves problems — is posed to the class for a brief oral exchange; written response goes to homework.

periods.teacher_notes: The extract questions require reading visual cues in the comic alongside the dialogue — draw students' attention to the panel showing the wife's posture as evidence of careful listening. The 'Oh, Oh!' exclamation from the kotwal and the 'Ssssh!' from the wife are good entry points for discussing how punctuation carries emotional weight in comics.
materials: Textbook pp.26–27 ('Let us think and reflect' I and II)

periods.activity_title: Listening Announcement and Speaking: Contractions and Safety Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.32): fill four blanks from the security guard's neighbourhood announcement.
Let us speak (p.33): discuss in pairs why safety matters and share three safety ideas.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the listening task: a security guard is making an announcement to a neighbourhood about robberies. Read the announcement text from p.38 aloud at a measured pace while students follow along with the blank-fill exercise on p.32.

Read the announcement a second time. Students fill in the four blanks (robbery; adults; safety; 100). Compare answers with a neighbour, then verify as a class by re-reading the relevant sentence from the announcement for each blank.

Introduce contractions using examples from the story ('I'm', 'It's', 'They're'). Model the pronunciation of the contracted forms listed on p.33 and have students repeat. Make clear that contracted forms belong to speech and expanded forms to formal writing.

Pairs discuss why it is important to keep their house and themselves safe (p.33), ticking suitable reasons and then sharing their views in complete sentences. Two or three pairs share aloud; the class briefly pools three ideas on how to stay safe at home.

periods.teacher_notes: The announcement connects directly to the story's context — a neighbourhood threat and a call for community alertness. When students fill in blank 4 (dial 100), confirm that the number is stated explicitly in the transcript and is not inference. For the speaking task, encourage quieter students with the same structured hints; paired format helps reduce hesitation.
materials: Textbook pp.32–33 ('Let us listen', 'Let us speak')

periods.activity_title: Narrative Retelling: The Man Tells His Neighbour

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.34): write a first-person narrative as the man, covering when, where, what, how, why.

time_bands.activity: Discuss the writing task: the man is retelling last night's events to a curious neighbour. Unpack the five prompts — when, where, what, how, why — and brainstorm with the class what details from the story belong under each heading. Write key phrases on the board.

Students write their narrative independently, starting from the given opening line on p.34. Circulate and give brief verbal guidance to those who struggle with sequencing the plan, the thief's entry, the coded conversation, and the kotwal's arrival.

Students pair up and read each other's drafts. They check: Has the partner included all five prompts? Is the voice clearly the man's (first person)? One piece of specific improvement feedback is shared orally between partners.

Two or three volunteers read their narratives aloud. The class comments on what details worked best and whether the story felt convincing from the man's point of view. Students make a final brief revision to their own piece.

periods.teacher_notes: The story gives students all the factual content they need — the challenge is first-person voice and sequencing. Students commonly list events without explaining how the coded-name plan worked; prompt them to explain the wife's signal system so the neighbour (and the reader) understands the cleverness of it. Peer response and revision are both included in this sitting so no separate draft is carried forward.

periods.activity_title: Contractions, Present Progressive Tense, and Adverbs

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.27): expand contracted forms I'm, It's, They're to full words.
Let us learn (p.28): expand contracted words and write original sentences for I'll, I'd, we'll, etc.
Let us learn (p.28): identify present progressive tense from story sentences; choose correct option.
Let us learn (p.29): fill blanks with correct present progressive forms in six sentences.

time_bands.activity: Open with the three highlighted sentences from the story on p.27 (I'm, It's, They're). Students write the full forms and identify the missing letter pattern — the apostrophe marks the omission. Establish the speech-vs-writing register rule.

Students work through the contraction expansion table on p.28, expanding I'll, I'd, we'll, that's, we're, don't, you'll and writing one original sentence for each. Pairs check each other's expansions before a class review.

Present the five story sentences on p.28 that use present progressive tense. Students choose the correct option (actions going on at the time of speaking) and articulate the rule: verb 'be' + main verb + -ing. Elicit further examples from the story.
Students fill in the six blanks on p.29 with the correct present progressive forms. Go through answers together, asking students to say aloud the full auxiliary + participle form before writing.

periods.teacher_notes: Contractions and present progressive are both drawn directly from the story's dialogue, so students can see real usage before the rule. A common error is omitting the auxiliary 'be' in present progressive (writing 'I studying' instead of 'I am studying') — display the auxiliary prominently and require students to say it aloud before writing.
materials: Textbook pp.27–29 ('Let us learn' contraction and tense tasks)

periods.activity_title: Adverbs in Context and Sentence Punctuation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.29–30): fill present progressive blanks from picture; fill adverb blanks (first box).
Let us learn (p.30): complete adverb table from three story sentences (closely, softly, very loudly).
Let us learn (p.31): exclamatory vs. interrogative sentences — choose correct option from story examples.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.31): punctuate four sentences; label each exclamatory or interrogative.

time_bands.activity: Students study the park-scene picture on p.29 and fill in present progressive verb forms, then fill the adverb blanks using the first word box (warmly, gracefully, smoothly, beautifully, funnily, quickly, hurriedly). Discuss how each adverb answers 'How?' for its verb.

Draw attention to the three story sentences on p.30 that contain adverbs of manner (closely, softly, very loudly). Students complete the adverb table, identifying the action and the adverb that qualifies it. Connect back to how the wife's choice of 'softly' vs. 'very loudly' drove the story's plot.

Introduce exclamatory and interrogative sentences using the story extracts on p.31. Students choose the correct emotion or function for each (tiredness / relief / asking a question). Clarify punctuation rules — exclamation mark vs. question mark — using the story dialogue as anchor examples.

periods.teacher_notes: Adverbs of manner from the story (closely, softly, loudly) are not incidental — they are the mechanism of the plot, so linking grammar to story logic helps retention. Students often conflate exclamatory and interrogative sentences when both carry strong emotion; use 'Oh, Oh!' and 'What should we do?' from the comic strip to show the structural difference.
materials: Textbook pp.29–31 ('Let us learn' adverb and sentence-type tasks)

periods.activity_title: Emergency Responses and Maze: Exploring Community Safety

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.34): find out who to call in six emergency situations; note down answers.
Let us explore (p.35): solve the maze to find the kotwal's path to catch the thief.

time_bands.activity: Recall the story's resolution: the kotwal, alerted by name, caught the thief. Ask the class: in real life, who do we call when something goes wrong? Briefly list two or three situations students suggest before moving to the textbook task.

Students work through the six emergency situations on p.34 — fire, someone getting hurt, a wounded animal, a suspicious person, a lost child, getting lost — noting who to call in each case. Pairs discuss and pool their answers, drawing on what they know from home or their neighbourhood.

Students solve the maze on p.35 individually, tracing the kotwal's correct path to reach the thief. Pairs compare solutions; if a disagreement arises, they trace together and identify where the paths diverge.

Brief class share: students name one emergency number or contact they learned today and explain when they would use it. Close by connecting the theme of community safety to the story — the kotwal's patrol made the couple's clever plan work.

periods.teacher_notes: The emergency-situations task works best when students draw on real local knowledge — encourage them to name the actual services in their area rather than generic answers. The maze is a quick kinesthetic close to the chapter that reinforces the story's resolution; if a student finishes early, ask them to write the path as a set of directions using directional adverbs.
materials: Textbook pp.34–35 ('Let us explore' emergency task and maze)

items.source_lo: Student identifies characters, events and textual details using a narrative comic-strip as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Husband-wife thief plan; kotwal Rama called by coded name; story map of problem and solution.
items.item_stem: In the story, the husband whispers a plan to his wife so that the thief cannot understand it. Which of the following correctly describes the husband's plan?

options.label: A
options.text: The husband will pretend to be asleep and let the wife handle the thief alone.

options.label: B
options.text: The wife will call the name 'Rama' at different volumes to signal where the thief is.

options.label: C
options.text: The wife will mention where the money is hidden to confuse the thief.

options.label: D
options.text: The wife will shout for help if she sees the thief move toward the door.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student missed the coded-name device and replaced it with a direct alarm signal.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student confused the husband's active role with passivity; he devises and whispers the plan.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student confused what the thief wished would happen with what the couple actually did.

items.source_lo: Student identifies characters, events and textual details using a narrative comic-strip as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Husband-wife thief plan; kotwal Rama called by coded name; story map of problem and solution.
items.item_stem: The couple's plan succeeds because of a coincidence between a name and a person. Explain how the name 'Rama' served two completely different purposes in the story — one for the couple and one that the thief did not realise. What does this tell you about the husband's cleverness?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The name 'Rama' was the couple's coded distress signal — its volume told the kotwal where the thief was — while the thief heard it only as the name of an unborn child. The husband's plan worked because it communicated danger to the kotwal without the thief suspecting anything, showing quick wit and an understanding of who was listening.

items.source_lo: Student retrieves specific information from a spoken announcement using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Security guard's neighbourhood announcement about robberies; safety instructions; emergency number 100.
items.item_stem: Listen to your teacher read the security guard's announcement. Then decide whether each of the following statements is True or False.

options.text: Adults are told to report suspicious activity to the children immediately.
The guard advises people to lock all doors and windows only when they leave the house.
The number to call in an emergency, according to the announcement, is 100.
The security guard's announcement is about robberies happening in the area.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the announcement explicitly states there are reports of robbery in the locality.
2. False — the announcement says children should inform adults, not the other way around.
3. False — the guard says to lock doors and windows at night AND when leaving the house, not only when leaving.
4. True — the announcement ends with 'Dial 100 in case of emergency.'

items.source_lo: Student retrieves specific information from a spoken announcement using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Security guard's neighbourhood announcement about robberies; safety instructions; emergency number 100.
items.item_stem: The security guard's announcement gives instructions to two different groups of listeners — adults and children. In one or two sentences, state what the guard specifically asks children to do and explain why this instruction might be especially useful in the neighbourhood described in the announcement.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The guard asks children to inform adults immediately if they notice anything suspicious, and not to talk to strangers or accept anything from them. This instruction is especially useful because children are often present in the neighbourhood and may notice unusual activity that adults miss, making them an important part of community safety.

items.source_lo: Student expresses opinions and shares practical ideas in paired conversation using guided speaking as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Importance of personal and household safety; three practical ideas for keeping safe.
items.item_stem: Describe to your partner two reasons why it is important for families to keep their homes safe. Use the story of the husband and wife in 'Rama to the Rescue' as one of your examples.

expected_elements: States two clear reasons for household safety in complete sentences.
References the story — the couple's vulnerability to the thief — as an example.
Uses simple linking words such as 'because', 'for example', 'also'.
Speaks clearly and at a volume the partner can hear.

items.source_lo: Student expresses opinions and shares practical ideas in paired conversation using guided speaking as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Importance of personal and household safety; three practical ideas for keeping safe.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are the kotwal Rama speaking to the villagers the morning after the arrest. Give a short speech of four to five sentences advising the villagers on three things they can do to keep themselves and their homes safe. Give a reason for at least one of your pieces of advice.

expected_elements: Adopts the role of the kotwal with appropriate formal or persuasive tone.
States three distinct practical safety measures.
Provides a reason or justification for at least one measure.
Delivers the speech in four to five complete, connected sentences.

items.source_lo: Student writes a first-person narrative retelling using a narrative text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Man retells theft night to neighbour: coded name plan, thief's entry, kotwal's arrival, resolution.
items.item_stem: Write a short paragraph (five to six sentences) as the wife in the story, describing the events of that night to a relative. Include what she noticed first, what her husband asked her to do, and how the kotwal arrived. Begin your paragraph with: 'My husband and I had just settled down for the night when I heard …'

expected_elements: Written in first person as the wife throughout the paragraph.
Includes the sound that first alerted her and what she told her husband.
Explains the coded-name signal and why the volume of calling mattered.
Describes the kotwal arriving and catching the thief as the resolution.
Uses past tense consistently and correct sentence punctuation.

items.source_lo: Student writes a first-person narrative retelling using a narrative text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Man retells theft night to neighbour: coded name plan, thief's entry, kotwal's arrival, resolution.
items.item_stem: The thief in the story is caught and taken away. Imagine you are the thief. Write a diary entry (six to eight sentences) describing your feelings during the time you were inside the house, what confused you about the couple's conversation, and what you wish you had done differently.

expected_elements: Written in first person as the thief, in diary-entry format with a date or greeting.
Describes his frustration at hearing talk about a child's name instead of money.
Shows he did not realise 'Rama' was the name of the actual kotwal on patrol.
Reflects on what he would have done differently, showing understanding of the couple's trick.
Uses past tense for events and present tense for feelings where appropriate.

items.source_lo: Student applies contractions, present progressive tense, and adverbs of manner drawn from the narrative in context.
items.source_context: Contractions from story dialogue; present progressive tense; adverbs closely, softly, loudly; exclamatory and interrogative sentences.
items.item_stem: The wife in the story uses adverbs of manner — softly and very loudly — to signal where the thief is. Rewrite the following two sentences by adding a suitable adverb of manner from the box and explain, in one sentence, what each adverb tells the reader about the character's action. Adverbs: closely, anxiously, hurriedly. (a) 'The husband listened to the sounds outside.' (b) 'The kotwal ran to the house when he heard his name.'

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Acceptable rewritings: (a) 'The husband listened closely / anxiously to the sounds outside' — 'closely' shows he was paying careful attention; 'anxiously' shows he was nervous and alert. (b) 'The kotwal hurriedly / quickly ran to the house when he heard his name' — 'hurriedly' shows he responded with urgency, fitting his role as a diligent officer on patrol.

items.source_lo: Student connects narrative themes to real-world community safety through hands-on inquiry.
items.source_context: Six emergency situations — fire, injury, wounded animal, suspicious person, lost child, getting lost.
items.item_stem: Just as the couple in the story knew to call on Rama the kotwal when they were in danger, we need to know who to call in different emergencies. For each situation below, write the name or service you would contact and one sentence explaining why that contact is the right choice.
items.visual_stimulus: | Situation | Who to contact | Why this contact |

expected_elements: Names an appropriate contact or service for each of the six situations.
Gives a one-sentence reason that matches the nature of the emergency.
Shows understanding that different emergencies require different helpers.
Connects at least one situation to the story's theme of community alertness.

items.source_lo: Student connects narrative themes to real-world community safety through hands-on inquiry.
items.source_context: Six emergency situations — fire, injury, wounded animal, suspicious person, lost child, getting lost.
items.item_stem: Design a small 'Safety Card' for your neighbourhood. It should list at least four emergency contacts with the situations in which each is used, and include one safety rule from the story of the husband and wife that your neighbours can follow. Present your card to the class.

expected_elements: Lists at least four emergency contacts with correct situations for each.
Includes one safety principle drawn from the story (e.g., alertness, community cooperation, or coded communication).
Card is clearly laid out so information is easy to read at a glance.
Student can explain the card's content when presenting to the class.
